name: Basal ganglia direct and indirect loops
summary: The basal ganglia form loops from the cortex through the striatum, pallidum and thalamus back to the cortex. In the direct pathway, cortical excitation of striatal neurons inhibits the internal pallidum and substantia nigra reticulata, releasing the thalamus and facilitating movement; in the indirect pathway, striatal neurons inhibit the external pallidum, which disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus, whose excitation of the internal pallidum suppresses the thalamus and movement. Dopamine from the substantia nigra compacta excites the direct (D1) and inhibits the indirect (D2) pathway, so its loss tips the balance toward inhibition (parkinsonism), while loss of striatal indirect neurons (Huntington) or of the subthalamic nucleus (hemiballismus) tips it toward excess movement.

origin.note: Glutamatergic input from the whole cortex to the striatum (motor cortex to the putamen, association cortex to the caudate, limbic cortex to the accumbens).

waypoints.note: excitatory node of the indirect pathway
pars compacta (dopamine to the striatum) and pars reticulata (output)
ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei

termination: Motor, premotor and supplementary motor cortex (motor loop), prefrontal cortex (associative loop) and anterior cingulate/orbitofrontal cortex (limbic loop) via the thalamus; brainstem targets (superior colliculus, pedunculopontine nucleus) via the nigra reticulata and pallidum.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Parkinsonism: bradykinesia, rigidity, rest tremor, postural instability

lesionEffectsByLevel.level: Striatum (Huntington disease, indirect pathway neurons lost first)

pearls: Too little dopamine or too much pallidal output: hypokinesia. Too little pallidal output: hyperkinesia
The subthalamic nucleus is the brake; the internal pallidum is the gate; dopamine sets the threshold
Basal ganglia lesions do not cause weakness, sensory loss or reflex change: they change the quality of movement
